title: A review of the scientific evidence on the impact of biologically salient frightening devices to protect crops from avian pests
full_text:
## **A review of scientific evidence on the impact of frightening devices to protect crops from**

## **avian pests**

Janice K. Enos[1,*] , Michael P. Ward[2] , Mark E. Hauber[1 ]

1Department of Evolution, Ecology, and Behavior, School of Integrative Biology, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, Illinois 61801, USA

2Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences, University of Illinois at UrbanaChampaign, Urbana, Illinois 61801, USA

*Corresponding Author:

Email: jkkelly2@illinois.edu

Address: 515 Morrill Hall, 505 S. Goodwin Ave., Urbana, IL 61801

- 1 **ABSTRACT**

- 2 Many bird species are considered agricultural pests and cause severe and costly damage to crops

- 3 worldwide. Crop producers use several methods to reduce damage by birds, with frightening

- 4 devices serving among the most popular approaches. Frightening devices, such as broadcast of

- 5 conspecific alarm calls or placing predator models in fields, are considered effective because

- 6 they can trigger antipredator behaviors that reduce foraging activities or abundances of target

- 7 birds locally. However, it remains unclear wh type of frightening device is most effective and

- 8 whether some frightening devices work best against certain bird species or on certain types of

- 9 crops. We reviewed the published scientific literature to fill in these knowledge gaps about using

- 10 frightening devices for crop protection against avian pests. We found 46 experiments evaluating

- 11 the impact(s) of frightening devices. However, only 26 experiments statistically tested their

- 12 results from which to draw conclusions. We found that alarm call playback, eyespot balloons,

- 13 and hawk-kites reduced avian abundance in all experiments. All experiments using alarm call

- 14 playbacks, eyespot balloons and automated flying vehicles (drones) effectively reduced crop

- 15 damage. However, only experiments on passerine birds and in row crops were well-represented

- 16 in these experiments. We discuss potential biases in the literature that may limit our

- 17 understanding of how birds respond to frightening devices and suggest future directions that

- 18 researchers might take to fill knowledge gaps.

- 19

- 20 _Key words:_ avian pests, crop damage, frightening devices, human-wildlife conflicts, predation

- 21 risk, wildlife management

- 22

- 23

## 24 **INTRODUCTION**

25 Globally, avian pests cause severe and costly damage to crops in many agricultural

- 26 systems (Linz et al. 2011). Australia, for example, loses US $300 million annually to crop

- 27 damage by 60+ bird species (Tracey et al. 2007). The United States experiences US $189 million 28 in fruit crop loss (Anderson et al. 2013) and US $47 billion in commercial grain crop loss due to 29 birds (Pimentel et al. 2005). Similar productivity loss to birds occurs in regions of Asia (Gupta et

- 30 al. 1998, Kale et al. 2014), Europe (Pinowski and Zając 1990, Hake et al. 2010), and Africa (de 31 Mey and Demont 2013). As a result, many crop producers prioritize reducing bird populations in 32 their agricultural fields to protect the crops from avian pests’ impacts (Avery and Werner 2017). 33 There are several methods crop producers use to reduce bird populations in and around 34 agricultural fields. Frightening devices, such as broadcast of target bird species’ conspecific

- 35 alarm calls or models of their predators, are considered effective because they can trigger

- 36 antipredator behaviors, such as increased vigilance, that can reduce foraging activity or repulse

- 37 flocks from fields altogether (Gilsdorf et al. 2002, Avery and Werner 2017). Indeed, several

- 38 behavioral ecology experiments on birds in non-agricultural contexts show that they reduce or

- 39 abandon foraging when perceived predation risk is high, such as when a predator model is

- 40 present (Cresswell et al. 2003, Devereux et al. 2006, Egan et al. 2020) or predator vocalizations

- 41 are broadcast (Barrera et al. 2011, Stanback and Powell 2011). Many frightening devices are less

- 42 costly and lower maintenance than other bird deterrents, such as gas cannons or netting (Linz et

- 43 al. 2011). Additionally, frightening devices often only require short-term maintenance or

- 44 operational duty cycle to attempt to deter birds from foraging in fields (Avery and Werner 2017). 45 Though frightening devices are popular and globally used (reviewed in Gilsdorf et al.

- 46 2002, Linz et al. 2011, Avery and Werner 2017), it is unknown whether specific types of

- 47 frightening devices are more effective than others at repulsing some or all avian pest species

- 48 from agricultural fields. Broadcast of conspecific alarm calls, for example, should be effective 49 against those species that are group living and use vocal communication to signal predation risk

- 50 to flock mates (Desrochers et al. 2002, Marler 2005). In contrast, predator models, a commonly

- 51 used frightening device (reviewed in Marsh et al. 1992, Avery and Werner 2017), may not deter 52 all avian pest species from agricultural fields because not all species consider the same predator

- 53 as high risk. For example, “hawk-kites,” which mimic genus _Buteo_ and _Accipiter_ birds-of-prey, 54 are marketed and widely used as a general, all-purpose deterrents for any bird species (reviewed

- 55 in Avery and Werner 2017). Yet, cranes (Family Gruidae) and geese (Family Anatidae), two

- 56 taxonomic groups with several pest species (Kirby et al. 1999, Dieter et al. 2014, Nilsson et al.

- 57 2016, Austin et al. 2018), may not respond to hawk-kite devices because _Buteo_ and _Accipiter_

- 58 hawks pose little risk to such large-bodied birds (Winkler et al. 2020). As a result, some

- 59 frightening devices could fail at protecting crops if applied with an “all-purpose” approach. 60 Frightening device effectiveness may also depend on the type of crop targeted for

- 61 protection. Row crops, orchards, and vineyards can differ considerably from one another, namely

- 62 in vegetation structure and spatial or temporal forage availability to birds (e.g., seasonal flowers,

- 63 seeds, fruits, or all three; Tracey et al., 2007, Kale et al. 2012, Dolbeer 2017). For example, one

- 64 study found orchards can attract several types of birds over the course of the growing season,

- 65 including nut-consumers and fruit-consumers, whereas vineyards only attract fruit consumers

- 66 (Luck et al. 2015). In contrast, row crops, such as corn and sunflower, have short vulnerability

- 67 windows that only overlap with a few avian pest species still present late growing season

- 68 (reviewed in Avery and Werner 2017). If frightening device effectiveness varies across bird

- 69 species, then not all crop types will be equally protected from avian pests.

- 70 Historically, studies evaluating frightening device effectiveness have tested a single

- 71 device at a time (e.g., Hothem and DeHaven 1982, Berge et al. 2007, Wang et al. 2020), and only

- 72 one or a few types of crops per study (e.g., Conover 1985, Khan et al. 2011, reviewed in Avery

- 73 and Werner 2017). Likewise, few studies test multiple bird species to assess if certain avian pest

- 74 species or taxonomic lineages are more sensitive to one type of frightening device than another

- 75 (e.g., conspecific alarm calls vs. predator model). With this single study approach, it is difficult

- 76 to evaluate whether specific types of frightening devices are more effective than others at

- 77 protecting crops from avian pests. It is also difficult to determine if certain species (or taxonomic 78 groups) are more sensitive to frightening devices than others, or if specific crop types are better 79 protected than others. A thorough review of the literature is crucial to assess which frightening 80 devices are most effective against which taxonomic groups of avian pests, and on what type of 81 crop. Doing so may aid crop producers in choosing the best option for their agricultural system. 82 We reviewed the published scientific literature to fill in these knowledge gaps about 83 using frightening devices to protect crops from avian pests. Though several reviews exist

- 84 synthesizing published studies qualitatively (e.g., Bomford and O’Brien 1990, Gilsdorf et al.

- 85 2002, Tracey et al. 2007, Avery and Werner 2017), no review to date has systematically queried

- 86 the literature regarding whether frightening devices work versus fail to protect crops from avian 87 pests. With results from our review, we address the three specific research questions:

- 88 (1) Is one type of frightening device more effective than others at reducing avian pest 89 populations in target fields, or at reducing crop damage, or both?

- 90 (2) Are frightening devices more effective against specific bird species or taxonomic 91 groups than others?

- 92 (3) Are specific types of crops (orchard, vineyard, or row crops) better protected with 93 frightening devices than others?

- 94 Our initial goal was to conduct a formal meta-analysis to address these questions, but we

- 95 found that too few studies reported information necessary to do so (see _Results_ ). We also wanted

- 96 to address patterns of habituation (Rankin et al. 2009) with our review, where birds may stop

- 97 responding to frightening devices over time after chronic exposure, but no experiments to date

- 98 have formally tested for habituation. Instead, we took a qualitative approach and summarized

- 99 patterns in the literature to address our research questions with. We then used our literature

- 100 review to determine which frightening devices, bird species, and crop types need more research

- 101 to help crop producers tailor their frightening device choices to best fit their agricultural systems.

- 102

- 103 **METHODS**

- 104 _Literature review_

- 105 We searched for studies on 15 Nov 2020 using ISI Web of Science and Google Scholar

- 106 databases (years 1900-2020). We conducted searches with the following terms: “bird” OR

- 107 “blackbird” OR “starling” OR “sparrow” OR “parrot” OR “parakeet” OR “goose” OR “crow”

- 108 OR “raven” OR “pigeon” OR “dove” OR “crane” AND (“deter*” OR “repel*” OR "frightening

- 109 device") AND (“crop” OR “agriculture” OR “orchard” OR “vineyard”). The specific birds were

- 110 included because we knew _a priori_ that they qualify as agricultural pests either worldwide or

- 111 regionally (e.g., Bomford and Sinclair 2002, Austin et al. 2013, Nilsson et al. 2016, Tracey et al.

- 112 2007, Linz et al. 2017). We also scanned the references section from relevant literature for

- 113 studies our search could have missed.

- 114 In our review, we only included experimental studies that employed one or more

- 115 frightening device treatment(s) and a control treatment group. Observational/correlational studies

- 116 are often confounded by other environmental factors that can influence crop damage and/or bird

- 117 abundances in agricultural fields (e.g., Pejchar et al. 2018, Heath and Long 2019). Studies that

- 118 did not report results quantitatively (e.g., response variable means or totals by treatment) were

- 119 excluded. We excluded studies that did not use biologically salient frightening devices

- 120 simulating high predation risk, including: “startling” devices such as reflective tape/metallic

- 121 objects or explosive/gas cannon devices (reviewed in Avery and Werner 2017), chemical

- 122 deterrents (reviewed in Mason and Clark 1992), ultrasonic broadcast (though most birds do not

- 123 have ultrasonic hearing; Ogochukwu et al. 2012), or frequency-masking “pink noise” (which

- 124 repulses birds by disrupting communication systems; Swaddle et al. 2016, Werrell et al. 2021).

- 125 We also excluded studies that took place in a laboratory, on wild populations trained to

- 126 experimental foraging trays, or in non-agricultural contexts (e.g., city parks, sporting fields,

- 127 airports).

- 128

- 129 _Data collection and evaluation_

- 130 We considered each combination of frightening device, crop type, and bird species

- 131 reported in a study as a separate “experiment” to extract data from. For example, if a study

- 132 reported results for one bird species, two frightening device types, and three different crop types,

- 133 then we considered it to generate n = 6 experiments from which to collect data (e.g., Khan et al.

- 134 2011). Similarly, if a study included several variants of a frightening device, such as three types

- 135 of predator models (e.g., Conover 1985), we included each variant as a separate experiment.

|136|Last, if multi-year studies reported results from each year separately, we considered each year as|
|---|---|
|137|a separate experiment. We then tallied the following data from each experiment:|
|138|(1) The taxonomic order of the target bird pest (hereafter “bird type”). Small|
|139|sample sizes precluded us from tallying by species or family (see_Results_),|
|140|which we recognize would be more appropriate. If experiments targeted|
|141|mixed-species flocks, we tallied as the order with the most (> 75%)|
|142|representative species reported in the flock.|
|143|(2) The type of frightening device used: “alarm call playback” (broadcast of|
|144|conspecific or heterospecific alarm calls, or distress calls many bird species|
|145|are known to respond negatively to), “hawk-kites” (aerial floating models|
|146|mimicking birds of prey known to depredate smaller bird species), “eyespot|
|147|balloons” (floating balloons mimicking a generic aerial predator),|
|148|“human/scarecrow models” (effigies of humans placed at one location),|
|149|“predator models” (effigies of predators placed at one location), or|
|150|“automated flying vehicles” (moving drones, remote-controlled helicopters,|
|151|hereafter “UAVs” as commonly referred to in the literature; Wang et al. 2020|
|152|and references therein). Some studies used different types of predator models|
|153|(e.g., Conover 1985), and some UAVs broadcast alarm calls or included|
|154|visual effigies (e.g., Wang et al. 2020). Because sample sizes were generally|
|155|small (see_Results_), we could not parse this variation into their own unique|
|156|categories (e.g., UAV with and without alarm call broadcast). We recognize|
|157|this methodology could have biased results and return to this point in the|
|158|_Discussion_.|

- 159 (3) The type of agricultural field tested as row crops, orchards, or vineyards 160 (“crop type” hereafter).

- 161 (4) The response variable collected to assess crop protection with, either damage 162 to crops in relation to treatments (“crop damage” hereafter, typically collected 163 as percentage of fruit or kernels missing from a plant), or reduction of bird 164 abundance or activity in relation to treatments (“bird abundance” hereafter).

- 165 As stated earlier, we tried but could not conduct a formal meta-analysis (Koricheva et al.

- 166 2013) to evaluate our tally data with because of low sample sizes (see _Results_ ). Furthermore,

- 167 very few studies reported means, variance, or other statistical test results, which are

- 168 quantitatively necessary for a meta-analysis (Nakagawa and Santos 2012). Instead, we generated

- 169 percentages of experiments where frightening device treatments significantly reduced crop

- 170 damage or bird abundances compared to control treatments. We further parsed these percentages

- 171 by frightening device type, bird type (i.e., avian order), and crop type to qualitatively address our

- 172 objectives with.

- 173

- 174 **RESULTS**

- 175 Our literature review returned 377 unique studies (Web of Science, n = 315; Google

- 176 Scholar, n = 62). Of these, 14 studies met our qualifications and yielded 46 experiments to

- 177 extract data from (summarized in Table 1, Appendix I). All experiments were conducted on

- 178 fields with a single crop. Most experiments used either playback of alarm calls (33%) or predator

- 179 models (30%) as frightening devices, whereas fewer used hawk-kites (17%), eyespot balloons

- 180 (11%), and UAVs (9%). No experiments used human models or scarecrows as frightening

- 181 devices. Most experiments were conducted in row crop fields (57%), followed by vineyards

- 182 (28%) and orchards (15%). Passerines (order Passeriformes) were targeted in most experiments 183 (70%), with parrots (order Psittaciformes) being the second-most targeted (28%), and geese

- 184 (order Anseriformes) were targeted the least (2%; Table 1). No other groups of birds known to

- 185 damage crops were targeted in this set of experiments (e.g., orders Gruiformes, or cranes, and

- 186 Columbiformes, or pigeons; Linz et al. 2015, Nilsson et al. 2016, Austin et al. 2018). Only 26

- 187 experiments (56%) reported statistical test results to evaluate our main objectives with (n = 15 188 testing crop damage reduction; n = 11 testing reduced bird abundance).

- 209 _Question 1: Is one type of frightening device more effective than others?_

- 210 Alarm call playbacks, eyespot balloons, and hawk-kites significantly reduced crop

- 211 damage in all experiments when tested (Fig. 1). Fewer experiments, but still a majority of those

- 212 conducted with predator models successfully reduced crop damage (Fig. 1). UAV use was not

- 213 successful at reducing crop damage in any experiments (Fig. 1). Alarm call playbacks, eyespot

- 214 balloons, and UAVs significantly reduced bird abundances in all experiments (Fig. 1).

- 239 More than half of experiments conducted in row crops found frightening devices to

## 251 DISCUSSION

- 252 We found that few studies have used scientific hypothesis-testing to assess if frightening

- 253 devices protect crops from avian pests. As a result, we discovered several knowledge gaps and

- 254 have a small sample size to address our research questions with (Fig. 4). Nonetheless, our

- 255 literature review provides support that frightening devices can reduce crop damage by birds, or

- 256 leastwise repulse birds from agricultural fields. In summary, we found alarm call playback,

- 257 eyespot balloons, and hawk-kites reduced target bird abundances in all experiments, whereas all

- 258 experiments that used alarm call playbacks, eyespot balloons, and UAVs effectively reduced

- 259 crop damage (Fig. 1). Only passerines were well-represented in the scientific experiments

- 260 identified for this review: passerine abundances were reduced in all experiments with frightening

- 261 devices, but experiments were not always successful at reducing crop damage by passerines (Fig.

- 262 2). Experiments on all three crop types (row crops, orchards, and vineyards) reduced bird

- 263 abundances when frightening devices were present. More than half of experiments in row crops

- 264 reduced crop damage by birds when frightening devices were present, but this was not the case

- 265 for vineyards (Fig. 3).

- 276 frightening device versus control treatments (n = 26) for our three areas of interest: frightening

- 277 device type (UAV i.e., aerial drone, predator model, hawk-kite, eyespot balloon, alarm call

- 278 playback, predator playback, human model), avian group (passerines, parrots, geese, doves,

- 279 cranes), and crop type (row, orchard, vineyard). Darker regions (black) represent larger sample

- 283

- 284 Despite the small sample sizes, results from our literature review may be useful to crop 285 producers. Many crop producers might perceive frightening devices as ineffective against avian

- 286 pests. Indeed, a survey among orchard and vineyard owners indicated that many producers did

- 287 not think frightening devices protected their crops against birds (Anderson et al. 2013). In the

- 288 same survey, many producers ranked acoustic playbacks and visual scare devices as only

- 289 “slightly effective” at reducing crop damage in their orchards and/or vineyards (Anderson et al. 290 2013), yet this is not what our literature review suggests. Specifically, we found that all

- 291 experiments using acoustic playbacks (alarm call playback) reduced bird abundances, and visual

- 292 scare devices (eyespot balloons, hawk-kites, and predator models) reduced crop damage in most

- 293 experiments (Fig. 2). However, our findings could only apply to row crop producers because

- 294 most scientific evidence supporting frightening devices comes from this crop type (Fig. 3).

- 295 Unfortunately, we do not yet have enough data to inform crop producers if frightening devices 296 are effective in vineyards and orchards. Indeed, only a single study on orchards (Tipton et al.

- 297 1989) and two on vineyards (McLennan et al. 1995, Wang et al. 2020) in our review statistically

- 298 analyzed their data to determine if frightening devices reduced crop damage by birds. More

- 299 experiments in orchards and vineyards would help inform these crop producers with scientific

- 300 evidence, who currently must rely on personal experience and/or anecdotal evidence upon which 301 to make their decisions.

- 302 Our literature review suggests a bias towards testing alarm call playbacks, eyespot

- 303 balloons, and predator models as the frightening device of choice. Alarm call playbacks and

- 304 eyespot balloons do appear to effectively reduce bird abundances on agricultural fields, as all

- 305 experiments yielded this result (Fig. 1). It is unknown, however, if these frightening devices also

- 306 reduce crop damage, because only one experiment per device type used statistical tests to assess

- 307 crop damage by treatment (alarm call playback: Manzoor et al. 2013; eyespot balloon: Tipton et

- 308 al. 1989). In contrast, crop damage reduction in response to predator models is well-tested

- 309 (relative to alarm call playbacks and eyespot balloons), but with mixed success depending on the

- 310 experiment (Fig. 1). Notably, all experiments statistically testing predator models came from

- 311 Conover (1985) which used both stationary and animated models of large owls (genus _Bubo_ ),

- 312 some of which were posed as if attacking crow models (genus _Corvus_ ). Variation in

- 313 effectiveness could be due to the different types of predator models, as only animated predator

- 314 models posed attacking model crows significantly reduced crop damage (Conover 1985). Is

- 315 motion or a “victim” model needed for predator models to effectively protect crops from birds?

- 316 This is likely so, because many bird species increase vigilance and reduce foraging when a bird-

- 317 of-prey is moving (as opposed to sitting still; Lima 1990, Whittingham et al. 2004, Tisdale and

- 318 Fernández-Juricic 2009, Nebel et al. 2019). Replications of Conover (1985) would help tease

- 319 apart what cue avian pests are responding to in predator models: is it the predator movement, the 320 presence of a “victim” model, or both?

- 321 Our literature review revealed that several frightening devices are understudied (Fig. 4).

- 322 To date, hawk-kites have only been scientifically tested in one study (Conover 1985). This is

- 323 surprising because hawk-kites are often commercially advertised as effective frightening devices

- 324 to target birds (but see Conover 1983). However, we found there is little scientific evidence to

- 325 support or refute this claim. At present we cannot assess from the reviewed evidence if hawk-

- 326 kites reduce crop damage or bird abundances in agricultural fields, despite their longstanding

- 327 presence in the literature (Conover 1979, Avery and Werner 2017). Additionally, we found some

- 328 plausible frightening devices missing from the literature entirely (Fig. 4). For example, no

- 329 studies have experimented with broadcast of predator vocalizations as frightening devices, which

- 330 several crop producers use to repulse birds from agricultural fields (J. K. Enos personal

- 331 observation). In ecological contexts, broadcast of predator vocalizations does impact avian

- 332 vigilance (e.g., Zanette et al. 2011) and repulses birds from habitat locations (e.g., Emmering and

- 333 Schmidt 2011). Future research should experimentally test the efficacy of frightening devices,

- 334 not only to fill in knowledge gaps, but also to provide more data to support or refute their 335 effectiveness.

- 336 Passerines were targeted the most in experiments testing frightening device effectiveness.

- 337 This bias towards passerines makes it difficult to determine which taxonomic group, if any, is

- 338 most sensitive to frightening devices. We found that parrots are underrepresented in experiments,

- 339 whereas geese, cranes, and pigeons are not represented at all (Fig. 2 and Fig. 4), all of which are

- 340 taxonomic groups with crop pest species (Kirby et al. 1999, Linz et al. 2011, Austin et al. 2018).

- 341 These results are surprising, because parrots and doves are major crop pests in South America 342 (Linz et al. 2015), and cranes are major crop pests Africa or Asia (Goroshko et al. 2008, Austin

- 343 et al. 2018). Perhaps parrots and cranes are underrepresented because of regional or global

- 344 limitations that precluded experimental studies. We found no frightening devices experiments

- 345 from South America and Africa, for example (Table 1). Geese may be underrepresented because

- 346 they could be highly specific crop pests. Geese are obligate herbivores and prefer to forage on

- 347 leafy crops, such as soy and cereal grain early in the growing season (Cummings 2016, Fox et al.

- 348 2016). Also, geese are only pests under certain population and environmental conditions, such as

- 349 when densities are high and standing water is prevalent in and around agricultural fields (Fox et

- 350 al. 2016). Taken together, there may be less of a necessity to test frightening devices on geese in

- 351 an agricultural context. In contrast, passerines appear to be widely encountered pests. The Red-

- 352 winged Blackbird ( _Agelaius phoeniceus_ ), for example is the most abundant bird species across

- 353 its range (Yasukawa and Searcy 2020) and is a major grain crop pest in North America (Linz et

- 354 al. 2017); House Sparrows ( _Passer domesticus_ ) and European Starlings ( _Sturnus vulgaris_ ) are

- 355 two globally invasive and abundant pests of many crop types (Fitzwater 1994, Dawson 2012,

- 356 Campbell et al. 2015, Linz et al. 2007, Shivambu et al. 2020).

- 357 Last, habituation was not tested in any studies included in our review, though most 358 authors (Table 1) provided anecdotal evidence of habituation in their systems. For example, 359 Hothem and DeHaven (1982) noted habituation to hawk-kites occurred ~3 weeks after 360 deployment in grape vineyards, whereas McClennan et al. (1995) observed habituation to

- 361 eyespot balloons within 1-3 weeks at grape vineyards. Some authors suggested that for crops

- 362 vulnerable to birds for only a short period of time, habituation to frightening devices may not be 363 a concern if birds are still responding during the short timeframe (Berge et al. 2007 and

- 364 references therein). However, for crops still vulnerable past the point of habituation, frightening 365 devices may not effectively protect crops against avian pests. This topic of habituation been

- 366 discussed extensively in other literature reviews (Bomford and O’Brien 1990, Avery and Werner 367 2017), but it is still unknown if: (1) habituation occurs to all frightening devices types or just

- 368 some, and (2) if habituation occurs, on average, in a matter of days or weeks. Future experiments

- 369 need to address these unknowns about habituation by monitoring changes in crop damage over 370 time in relation to frightening devices ( _sensu_ McClennan et al. 1995).

- 371 In conclusion, our literature review is a “call to arms” for researchers to continue testing 372 which frightening devices work against avian pests. Importantly, future studies should include

- 373 control treatments and statistical hypothesis-testing in their experimental design. Additionally, 374 future studies should collect data on both crop damage and bird abundance to compare, as

- 375 reduced abundance may not necessarily mean reduced crop damage. Even if bird abundances are 376 reduced, those remaining birds could habituate to frightening devices and resume foraging on

- 377 crops despite the frightening device present (Bomford and O’Brien 1990, Avery and Werner 378 2017). Designing experiments to fill in the knowledge gaps we identified here, or replicating

- 379 existing experiments, are fruitful directions to determine what, when, and where frightening

- 380 devices might prevent crop damage by birds.
